standard_prerequisites.name: Cardinal exponentiation
standard_prerequisites.statement: For cardinals a and b, the power a to the b is the cardinality of the set of functions from b to a.
standard_prerequisites.use: Both bijections are built on the level of these function sets and establish the identities of their cardinalities (592-609).

standard_prerequisites.name: Cardinal addition and multiplication
standard_prerequisites.statement: The sum of two cardinals is the cardinality of their disjoint sum and the product is the cardinality of the Cartesian product of the two sets.
standard_prerequisites.use: The first law is proved by splitting a function on the disjoint sum, and the second by indexing along a Cartesian product (593-606).

standard_prerequisites.name: Bijection
standard_prerequisites.statement: A bijection is a function that is injective and surjective, and two sets have the same cardinality when a bijection between them exists.
standard_prerequisites.use: Each half of the proof ends by identifying the constructed map as a bijection between the two function sets (596-600, 607-609).

core_obligations: For the first law consider an arbitrary function f from the disjoint sum of the cardinals b and c into a (592-593).
Split f into its two components, the function f_b on b and the function f_c on c obtained by restricting f to the two summands (594-596).
Show the splitting map is a bijection from the function set on the disjoint sum onto the product of the two function sets, so the cardinalities agree and the first law follows (596-600).
For the second law consider an arbitrary function f from c into the set of functions from b to a, so each value f of gamma is itself a function on b (602-605).
Curry f into the function f-star on the Cartesian product of b and c defined by evaluating the gamma-component at beta (605-606).
Show the currying map is a bijection from the function set on c into the function set on b onto the function set on the Cartesian product, which is the second law (607-609).

proof_roadmap.step: Split a function on a disjoint sum into its two summand components.
Identify the splitting map as a bijection and read off the first law.
Curry a function whose values are functions into a function of two arguments.
Identify the currying map as a bijection and read off the second law.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's proposition at source lines 582-589: exponentiation of cardinals distributes over cardinal addition in the exponent and composes in the exponent. The 19-line proof (591-610) proves both laws by exhibiting explicit bijections rather than by quoting arithmetic of cardinals: for the first law it splits a function defined on the disjoint sum of two cardinals into its two components and claims the splitting map is a bijection onto the product of the two function sets (592-600); for the second law it curries a function of two arguments into a function into a function set and claims the currying map is again a bijection (602-609). The statement records neither the splitting nor the currying, and both bijectivity claims have to be verified on the level of functions.
